text.arabic_uthmani: قَالُوا۟ يَٰٓأَبَانَا ٱسْتَغْفِرْ لَنَا ذُنُوبَنَآ إِنَّا كُنَّا خَٰطِـِٔينَ

words.gloss_range: reported saying, here a completed collective speech act opening quoted confession
words.root_gloss_range: saying, assertion, communication, and outward expression of inner meaning; locally a speech-reporting verb with quoted complement
words.prose: {{ar:قَالُوا۟}} ({{tr:qālū}}) makes the brothers one grammatical speaking group before the plea begins. The perfect speech form presents the utterance as a settled response, not a tentative attempt, and the quoted content then moves through address, petition, and confessed grounds. Because the same speech architecture had carried earlier dealings with their father, the word now helps reverse those scenes: the voices that once managed the narrative now answer Jacob with public acknowledgment, including echoes of the confession to Joseph (12:91) and the earlier father-address pattern (12:17).

topics.headline: collective speech starts the plea
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the plea begins as one collective utterance, not as a private request by one brother.
topics.reason: The 3mp perfect verb and quoted-complement attachment identify the brothers as the collective speakers of the whole quoted plea.

topics.headline: settled speech, not commanded speech
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the confession enter the scene as the brothers' own completed speech act.
topics.reason: The form is a perfect declarative speech verb, not an imperative telling the brothers what to say.

topics.headline: speech carries hidden guilt outward
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the repair happens through accountable speech: the concealed history is voiced before Jacob.
topics.reason: The verb governs the vocative, imperative petition, and causal confession as its quoted complement.

topics.headline: earlier speech patterns reverse
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the same kind of father-directed speech return with the opposite moral force, from earlier management of the story to confession.
topics.reason: The rows give concrete same-surah anchors for speech to Jacob, Jacob's prior speech, and the confession before Joseph.

topics.headline: sound opens into appeal
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the long speech ending flow into the open father-address cadence.
topics.reason: The sound row adds a local pacing payoff as the speech verb is immediately followed by the vocative opening.

words.prose: {{ar:يَا}} ({{tr:yā}}) makes Jacob the immediate addressee before the command appears. It launches the quotation through relationship rather than demand, so the imperative that follows is heard inside a filial appeal. The long vocative onset also slows the entry into the petition, letting address and tenderness precede the request.

topics.headline: direct address selects Jacob
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the petition is routed through direct address to Jacob, not reported as a general wish.
topics.reason: The vocative particle governs the father noun and opens the quoted plea by selecting the addressee.

topics.headline: vocative softens the command
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the command approached as a relational appeal before it becomes directive.
topics.reason: The particle precedes the father-address and imperative, allowing urgency and tenderness to be read from the local confession setting.

words.gloss_range: our father, vocative five-noun form with first-person plural possession
words.root_gloss_range: father, progenitor, source, and kinship authority; locally fatherhood, not the refusal-root alternative
words.prose: {{ar:أَبَانَا}} ({{tr:abānā}}) fixes the command socially before it is spoken: the addressee is Jacob as father, not an unnamed elder or merely a prophet in narration. Its five-noun vocative shape marks the direct address, while the attached plural suffix makes the relationship collective: the brothers say our father as the same group that will say for us, our sins, indeed we, and we were. The fatherhood root is the locally selected sense; the root-dispute material only sharpens that this is kinship authority, not a refusal field. Because the request is to ask forgiveness, the word also makes Jacob the petitioned father-intercessor, a role echoed by inverted father-forgiveness scenes such as Abraham's prayer for his father (26:86; 9:114) and by the repeated father-address formula inside Surah 12 (12:11; 12:17; 12:63).

topics.headline: case form marks direct address
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the father noun grammatically locked into vocative address before the imperative.
topics.reason: The QAC and attachment evidence identify the word as a five-noun vocative governed by the preceding particle.

topics.headline: our father binds speakers to Jacob
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the guilty speakers invoke a definite family bond as a group, not an abstract moral authority.
topics.reason: The possessive suffix makes the father relation definite and ties the addressee to the same plural group that speaks through the rest of the ayah.

topics.headline: fatherhood is the selected root field
topics.reader_payoff: The reader keeps the origin and kinship authority of fatherhood without shifting the local word into an unrelated refusal sense.
topics.reason: The local surface is aligned to the fatherhood root; root-dispute evidence may qualify the lexical background but cannot replace the vocative father sense.

topics.headline: father relation frames intercession
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees why the brothers ask Jacob to seek forgiveness: the plea is mediated through paternal authority.
topics.reason: The vocative addressee controls the singular imperative that follows, making Jacob the requested seeker of forgiveness.

topics.headline: familiar address returns changed
topics.reader_payoff: The reader recognizes the same father-address formula returning with a penitent function rather than a strategic one.
topics.reason: The rows give same-surah father-address anchors and cross-passage father-forgiveness anchors that illuminate but do not control the local parse.

topics.headline: open vowels sustain the appeal
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the father-address stretched before the command, reinforcing the appeal register.
topics.reason: The sound row adds local cadence payoff to the vocative phrase.

words.gloss_range: seek forgiveness, locally a singular imperative asking Jacob to seek covering for the brothers' sins
words.root_gloss_range: covering, concealing, protecting, forgiving, and pardoning; locally activated through Form X seeking/requesting forgiveness
words.prose: {{ar:ٱسْتَغْفِرْ}} ({{tr:istaghfir}}) is the ayah's imperative hinge: the plural brothers ask one father to seek forgiveness for them. The Form X shape matters because Jacob is not cast as the independent forgiver; he is asked to seek the covering that belongs ultimately to God, which the next ayah answers when Jacob promises to seek forgiveness (12:98). The verb also fills both sides of the petition, with {{ar:لَنَا}} ({{tr:lanā}}) naming the beneficiaries and {{ar:ذُنُوبَنَا}} ({{tr:dhunūbanā}}) naming the object. The root's covering image survives locally as the requested covering over exposed fault, and same-surah links to forgiveness for sin (12:29; 12:92; 12:98) make this the middle step in a forgiveness arc.

topics.headline: Jacob is asked to seek
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the mediation structure: plural offenders ask one father to seek forgiveness rather than claiming it directly.
topics.reason: The verb is a singular masculine Form X imperative controlled by the father vocative, with Jacob as requested seeker.

topics.headline: beneficiary and object are explicit
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the plea name both who needs benefit and what needs forgiveness.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence marks the following prepositional phrase as beneficiary complement and the sin noun as explicit direct object.

topics.headline: forgiveness carries covering imagery
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can feel forgiveness as protective covering over exposed guilt while keeping the local sense as seeking forgiveness.
topics.reason: The root image is relevant lexical pressure, but the local Form X imperative selects seeking forgiveness rather than a physical covering artifact.

topics.headline: request creates the next response
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees this verb as the pivot between Joseph's prior forgiveness and Jacob's next-ayah promise.
topics.reason: The supplied rows give concrete same-surah forgiveness anchors before and after this request.

topics.headline: sin and forgiveness pair tightly
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the request is not generic mercy; it invokes the recognizable pairing of forgiveness with named sins.
topics.reason: The local object and cooccurrence rows support the forgiveness-for-sin pattern, specialized here through Jacob.

topics.headline: address links into command
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the father-address and imperative as one continuous appeal.
topics.reason: The sound row concerns the transition from the preceding vocative into the command.

words.gloss_range: for us, with lām marking beneficiary rather than object

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: seek forgiveness for us for our sins

words.prose: {{ar:لَنَا}} ({{tr:lanā}}) marks the brothers as beneficiaries of the requested act, not as the object forgiven. Placed before {{ar:ذُنُوبَنَا}} ({{tr:dhunūbanā}}), it makes the plea first name who needs mercy and then what burdens them. The attached plural pronoun also turns Jacob's prior you-address in 12:96 into the brothers' own for-us petition, while the repeated nā sound binds benefit, owned sins, emphatic assertion, and past state into one confession chain.

topics.headline: for us names the beneficiaries
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the word identifies who receives the benefit while the sins are named separately.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence marks the prepositional phrase as beneficiary complement of the imperative.

topics.headline: the accused group says for us
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the rebuked sons take the posture of recipients needing mercy.
topics.reason: The suffix refers to the speaking brothers and recasts the prior addressees as self-confessing beneficiaries.

topics.headline: benefit precedes burden
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the ordering: the plea first says for us, then names our sins.
topics.reason: The local order places the beneficiary phrase between the imperative and its explicit object.

topics.headline: nā links the confession
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the same plural self-reference recur across benefit, sins, assertion, and state.
topics.reason: The sound row names the repeated first-person plural ending across adjacent confession words.

words.gloss_range: our sins, an explicit plural object of the forgiveness request
words.root_gloss_range: sin, offense, guilt, and trailing consequence; locally plural owned sins brought under a forgiveness request
words.prose: {{ar:ذُنُوبَنَا}} ({{tr:dhunūbanā}}) gives the petition its explicit object: the brothers do not ask for vague favor but name our sins. The plural and possessive suffix make the burden both accumulated and owned by the same speakers who called Jacob our father. The root image of a trailing consequence remains useful here because the sins are what follow them into the scene and must be covered by the forgiveness request. Same-surah and wider formula rows reinforce the pairing of sins with forgiveness (12:29; 3:16; 3:147; 14:10), while the local order lets the word land heavily after for us.

topics.headline: our sins names the object
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the petition explicitly names the moral burden to be forgiven.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence identifies the plural noun as the direct object of the imperative, with first-person plural possession.

topics.headline: plural guilt is accumulated
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the confession is not narrowed to one incident; it gathers owned offenses as a plural burden.
topics.reason: The local form is a plural abstract noun functioning as direct object, not a partitive phrase.

topics.headline: sins trail the speakers
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can picture the sins as consequences still following the brothers into the request, while the local gloss remains sins.
topics.reason: The tail image is retained as lexical pressure, but the local noun directly denotes sins or offenses.

topics.headline: named sins call for forgiveness
topics.reader_payoff: The reader recognizes the phrase as part of a broader confession-and-forgiveness pattern rather than an isolated noun.
topics.reason: The rows give formulaic and cooccurrence evidence linking the sin noun with forgiveness language.

topics.headline: one fault becomes collective burden
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the same-surah sin-and-forgiveness field shift from an earlier individual fault to the brothers' collective confession.
topics.reason: The concrete 12:29 rows support a same-surah contrast without changing the local object relation.

topics.headline: object lands after for us
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the petition become specific when the heavy plural object arrives after the beneficiary phrase.
topics.reason: The rows concern the local sequence and cadence by which the object completes the petition.

words.gloss_range: indeed we, emphatic particle fused with first-person plural pronoun
words.prose: {{ar:إِنَّا}} ({{tr:innā}}) turns the final clause into explicit grounds for the request. The brothers put themselves under emphatic scope before the copula and predicate arrive, so the confession is not a loose emotional addition but the asserted reason Jacob should seek forgiveness. Its fused particle and plural pronoun compress emphasis with self-reference, and the nasal echo with {{ar:كُنَّا}} ({{tr:kunnā}}) makes indeed we and we were sound like one continuous self-incrimination.

topics.headline: indeed we foregrounds admission
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the brothers assert their guilt before the predicate names it.
topics.reason: The particle takes the fused first-person plural pronoun as its governed noun and introduces the predicate content.

topics.headline: confession explains the request
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the final clause as the stated reason for seeking forgiveness, not as an unattached afterthought.
topics.reason: The clause analysis marks the final clause as explanation for the imperative request.

topics.headline: full emphasis makes it direct
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the admission before Jacob as direct and emphatic, even against the earlier confession pattern (12:91).
topics.reason: The rows contrast this full emphatic opening with the earlier confession frame while preserving the local causal confession.

topics.headline: nasal echo joins assertion to state
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears assertion and state bound by adjacent plural nasal forms.
topics.reason: The local sequence places two adjacent nā-bearing forms at the start of the confession clause.

words.gloss_range: we were or had been, locally a copular past-state verb linking the speakers to the sinner predicate
words.root_gloss_range: being, becoming, existence, and state; locally a copular frame for moral self-description
words.prose: {{ar:كُنَّا}} ({{tr:kunnā}}) makes the brothers' guilt a predicated state, not only a past action. The perfect copula carries the plural we into {{ar:خَاطِئِينَ}} ({{tr:khāṭiʾīna}}), so the final clause becomes a full self-description: indeed we had been sinners. That form also reverses earlier denial grammar such as we were not thieves (12:73), and it repeats the confession before Joseph (12:91) in front of Jacob. The adjacent nā cadence with {{ar:إِنَّا}} ({{tr:innā}}) keeps assertion, state, and collective responsibility sonically joined.

topics.headline: guilt is predicated as state
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the brothers confess what they had been, not merely something they once did.
topics.reason: The verb is a copular kāna form whose predicate complement is the following active participle.

topics.headline: we is inside the state
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees collective responsibility carried into the very verb that predicates guilt.
topics.reason: The first-person plural subject is fused into the copula and controlled by the speakers in the quote.

topics.headline: being field adds state pressure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can feel guilt as a condition the brothers inhabited while keeping the local grammar as copular predication.
topics.reason: Broader being and status semantics can color the copular use, but the local function is not a lexical place noun or independent existential claim.

topics.headline: denial grammar becomes confession
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the same copular grammar move from self-defense to self-indictment, and from Joseph to Jacob.
topics.reason: The rows give concrete same-surah anchors for denial, confession, and repeated copular guilt language.

topics.headline: copula plus predicate forms admission
topics.reader_payoff: The reader recognizes the clause as a compact admission formula that grounds the petition.
topics.reason: The copula with the guilt predicate is marked as explanatory clause and has same-surah cooccurrence support.

topics.headline: copula turns emphasis into predicate
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the copula as the hinge carrying emphatic we into the heavy final guilt word.
topics.reason: The word stands between the emphatic particle and predicate, with repeated nā sound leading into the final label.

words.gloss_range: sinners or culpable wrongdoers, locally an active-participle predicate complement of the copula
words.root_gloss_range: culpable error, sin, and deviation from the right course; locally a plural agentive self-label, not innocent mistake
words.prose: {{ar:خَاطِئِينَ}} ({{tr:khāṭiʾīna}}) is the ayah's final landing: the petition ends by naming the brothers themselves as culpable agents. As an accusative plural predicate of {{ar:كُنَّا}} ({{tr:kunnā}}), it completes the confession as identity-like self-description, not merely an object of regret. The active participle and plural agreement move from our sins to the ones who were sinners, and the culpability field refuses to reduce the admission to innocent mistake. Its recurrence from the brothers' confession before Joseph (12:91), its links with other wrongdoer labels (12:29; 28:8), and the next-ayah answer through the forgiving attribute (12:98) make the closing word carry both self-indictment and forward pressure toward forgiveness. Qiraat and sound rows are best kept as texture: a hamza-bearing surface or smoothed reading changes the acoustic pressure, not the culpable predicate.

topics.headline: final predicate names the speakers
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the final word complete the copular confession by predicating guilt of the brothers.
topics.reason: The noun is the accusative predicate complement of the preceding copula.

topics.headline: agentive plural makes guilt collective
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the confession move from owned sins to the brothers as the ones characterized by culpable deviation.
topics.reason: The active participle agrees with the plural speakers and functions as a self-applied predicate label.

topics.headline: word choice refuses mere mistake
topics.reader_payoff: The reader understands the admission as knowing moral culpability rather than miscalculation.
topics.reason: The CRITICAL lexical rows distinguish culpable sin from innocent error, and no guardrail evidence contradicts that local force.

topics.headline: wrongdoing has path-deviation pressure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the label as culpable departure from the right course while keeping the local gloss as sinners.
topics.reason: The deviation image gives lexical color, but the local function is the active-participle sinner predicate.

topics.headline: bare predicate is direct
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the brothers identify themselves directly rather than placing themselves among a class.
topics.reason: The local predicate is bare after the copula, contrasting with the class-mediated expression supplied for 12:29.

topics.headline: sound shifts, culpability remains
topics.reader_payoff: The reader can notice hamza pressure and its smoothed variant without changing the meaning of the confession.
topics.reason: Variant and phonetic evidence affects recitational texture but does not alter the predicate's culpability.

topics.headline: self-label repeats and awaits answer
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the same guilt label complete the confession before Jacob and press forward to the forgiving answer in 12:98.
topics.reason: The rows provide concrete recurrence and forward-answer anchors for the final guilt predicate.

topics.headline: ayah closes on culpability
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the ayah end not on the request itself but on the brothers' self-indicting label.
topics.reason: The word is the final predicate of the ayah and gathers morphology, recurrence, variant texture, and closure.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The vocative to "our father" and the imperative "seek forgiveness for us" join paternal relation to an acknowledged offense.
baseline_models.mechanism: The speakers identify the father as a repairing, nurturing intermediary and ask him to seek a covering that protects confessed offenders from the effects of their deliberate wrongs.

activation_trace.role: Fatherhood supplies nurture and repair, making the addressee a relational intermediary.
Forgiveness covers the offense and protects its owner from its effect; the imperative assigns the requested act.
The plural object names the speakers' acts as guilt rather than mere misfortune.
Their final self-predicate marks culpable, deliberate wrongdoing rather than an accidental miss.

changed_reading.after: They confess shared culpability and enlist paternal care to petition for protection from its effects.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The request to cover "our sins" is followed by a past-state clause, "we were wrongdoers."
baseline_models.mechanism: The covering image in forgiveness combines with the tail or last-part image latent in sins: the plea seeks containment of wrongdoing's remainder even as the speakers cast culpability as a prior state.

activation_trace.role: A protective covering supplies the proposed containment of what remains exposed.
The tail and last-part image turns sins into consequences that trail behind their acts.
Past occurrence locates their culpable condition in narrated time without proving that its effects have ended.
Deliberate culpability keeps the aftermath model from reducing their wrong to accident.

changed_reading.before: They ask pardon for a set of past deeds.
changed_reading.after: They ask that the still-trailing remainder of a culpable past be covered so it does not govern the present.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: Collective "they said" opens a vocative, an imperative request, and a first-person-plural admission.
baseline_models.mechanism: The utterance is both confession and negotiated repair: the group states shared liability, addresses the injured family authority, and proposes the father's petition as the next action.

activation_trace.role: Negotiation in a matter makes the collective saying a proposal for how repair should proceed.
The paternal address construction identifies the person from whom the proposed action is requested.
Seeking forgiveness gives the negotiated speech a concrete reparative action.
Shared guilt is the admitted liability on which the request is based.

changed_reading.after: Their collective confession also negotiates a next step: acknowledgment from them and an intercessory act from the father.

context_deltas.mechanism: The same group has just located old error in the father; restored sight and vindicated knowledge reverse that judgment. Addressing him as father and calling themselves wrongdoers now transfers epistemic authority back to the person they dismissed.

activation_trace.role: The paternal relation anchors the reversal in renewed recognition of his repairing authority.
Missing the right direction becomes the speakers' self-description after they assigned deviation to him.
Deviation from right direction supplies the immediately preceding predicate imposed on the father.
Ancient duration intensifies their prior accusation as an entrenched judgment rather than a passing doubt.
Return to a former condition supplies the sensory reversal that overturns their accusation.
Restored ocular sight visibly confirms the father's previously discounted perception.
Knowledge disclosed to its knower frames the father's explicit contrast between what he knows and what they do not.

structural_cues: 12:95 predicates old deviation of the father; 12:96 restores his sight and vindicates his knowledge; 12:97 shifts the error predicate to the speakers.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies accusation, sensory reversal, and self-accusation; I infer a deliberate transfer of epistemic authority back to the father. A live alternative is sequential remorse without a crafted predicate reversal.

changed_reading.before: They approach a father who happens to be the injured parent.
changed_reading.after: They retract an epistemic hierarchy: the father they called chronically mistaken is vindicated, and they now place error in themselves while asking him to act.

context_deltas.mechanism: The father's answer repeats their forgiveness verb but defers its performance and directs it to his Lord, named forgiving and merciful. Fatherhood is therefore an intercessory link, while the split repair and growth images of lordship make forgiveness restorative rather than a bare cancellation.

activation_trace.role: Paternal nurture supplies the human link in the requested intercession.
Their imperative initiates the request for protection from the offense's effect.
The father's promised petition and the divine forgiving attribute complete the intercessory chain.
Repair, nurture, and completion make the Lord the effective agent of restored moral condition.
The secondary mapped image of nourishment and growth keeps open a maturation reading of forgiveness.
Tender mercy qualifies the divine response toward which the father directs their plea.

structural_cues: The future particle in 12:98 delays the father's petition, and "my Lord" identifies its ultimate addressee.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies repetition, futurity, lordship, forgiveness, and mercy; I infer a children-to-father-to-Lord chain and restorative direction. The delay may instead be temporal discretion without a staged repair process.

changed_reading.before: The father is asked to secure pardon.
changed_reading.after: His answer relocates efficacy beyond himself: he will carry their plea to the nurturing Lord whose forgiveness and mercy can repair them.

context_deltas.mechanism: The sequence moves from confession and promised intercession to entering, being gathered into shelter, and receiving safety. The plea can therefore be read as threshold speech that precedes reincorporation into a protected family space.

context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies an immediate plea-response-entry sequence; I infer that confession functions as a social threshold for reentry. The live alternative is chronology only, with no causal dependence between forgiveness and admission.

changed_reading.before: The plea concerns an inward moral debt.
changed_reading.after: The plea also prepares a passage from estrangement into sheltered, trusted family membership.

context_deltas.mechanism: The focus gives the brothers an unqualified first-person admission of culpability, while 12:100 describes satanic incitement operating in the interval between brothers. structural_cues: The brothers say "our sins" and "we were wrongdoers" in 12:97; Joseph later says the incitement occurred between him and his brothers in 12:100.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies self-attribution, an inciter, and a damaged fraternal interval; I infer layered causation and relational repair. A live alternative is that Joseph's incitement language is gracious mitigation rather than a causal supplement to their account.

changed_reading.before: The brothers confess acts attributable only to themselves.
changed_reading.after: They retain full confessed agency inside a layered account of incitement, with forgiveness aimed at repairing the bond that the wrongdoing split.

context_deltas.mechanism: The focus root image of a sin as a trailing end is activated by later language of outcome, punishment after guilt, non-repulsion, and criminal liability. The plea seeks interruption of a consequence chain, not denial that the chain was earned.

activation_trace.role: Protective covering supplies the requested interruption of exposed consequences.
The tail or last part makes guilt something that can continue after the originating act.
The end and outcome image extends the focus's trailing remainder into an eventual result.
Punishment following guilt makes the inferred consequence arrow explicit while leaving its application open.
Repulsion and prevention supply the action that the closing warning denies once punitive force arrives.

structural_cues: 12:109 asks readers to inspect the outcome of predecessors; 12:110 says punitive force is not repelled from the criminal people.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies tail, outcome, punishment-after-guilt, and non-repulsion images; I infer that the plea aims to stop an earned aftermath. The later warning may instead be a general coda with no direct comment on the brothers' request.

changed_reading.before: Forgiveness removes a backward-looking moral entry.
changed_reading.after: Forgiveness is sought as protection that can interrupt the forward-moving aftermath of confessed guilt before it hardens into punitive outcome.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This is surprising because it uses the form-distant mapped target ق ل ل under focus ق و ل; it remains anchored to the opening speech verb and visibly changes the social posture of the utterance. Render it only as a secondary sound/root-split activation, not as the lexical meaning of "they said."
surprising_valid_outliers.focus_anchor: The opening collective speech verb carries a packet-supplied secondary mapping to smallness and diminution.

activation_trace.role: Smallness, paucity, and abasement make the act of speaking an exploratory lowering of the group before the father.
The direct paternal address gives that self-lowering a concrete relational direction.

changed_reading.before: The speech verb neutrally introduces their confession.
changed_reading.after: At a contained split-root level, the act of speaking also performs self-diminishment before the father whose judgment they had resisted.

surprising_valid_outliers.containment: This cross-root material analogy is surprising: protective غفر and punitive غاشية are not lexical equivalents. It remains valid because both packet branches explicitly supply covering images and the focus asks for one before the context warns of the other. Render it as an image-level contrast, never as an etymological identification.
surprising_valid_outliers.focus_anchor: The focus imperative activates forgiveness as a protective covering over confessed sins.

activation_trace.role: A covering that protects supplies the desired enclosure around the speakers and their exposed guilt.
An overlying covering supplies the feared material counterpart: an enveloping visitation rather than protection.
The parallel mapped covering image reinforces that the contrast arises from packet imagery across both resolved targets.
Painful punishment identifies what the feared contextual covering carries.

changed_reading.before: They seek forgiveness before a possible punishment.
changed_reading.after: At the image level, they seek the protective covering of forgiveness lest the covering that reaches them instead be punitive.

strongest_changes: The sequence reverses the locus of error: the father accused of old deviation becomes sighted and knowing, while the speakers now predicate culpability of themselves.
The father's answer turns the plea into a deferred children-to-father-to-Lord chain governed by repair, forgiveness, and mercy.
Entry, shelter, safety, and the named fraternal rupture make the confession a possible threshold of family reincorporation rather than only private remorse.
Later outcome and criminal-liability branches activate sins as trailing consequences, while a contained cross-root reading contrasts protective and punitive coverings.
summary.what_was_special: The focus supports coexisting juridical, relational, temporal, and material readings. Split mappings add a restrained self-diminishment reading to the speech act and a growth dimension to divine repair; the context then changes who is judged mistaken, where forgiveness becomes effective, and what social and consequential work the plea may perform.
remaining_uncertainties: The confession-response-entry order may be causal thresholding or only narrative succession.
The past-state construction does not by itself prove that the speakers claim a completed change of identity.
Joseph's incitement account may distribute causation or may graciously mitigate blame without revising it.
The competing-coverings model is a cross-root image analogy and must remain exploratory.

reader_a.activated_readings_md: 1. **The sons now seek paternal mediation for trailing consequences.** غ ف ر B002, ذ ن ب B001/B002 (sin; trailing rear), and خ ط ء B002 move from confession to requested shielding. I infer that wrongdoing continues behind the completed act as consequence, and the father’s prayer is sought to cover that tail.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: Later 12:98 accepted the request as a promised petition and placed its efficacy under divine forgiveness and mercy.

reader_a.activated_readings_md: 1. **Wrongdoing recognized through the consequence that trails it.** `ذ ن ب:B001` is sin as a culpable act with bad consequence; dormant `ذ ن ب:B002` is the tail or trailing end of a thing. The plea comes only after the brothers’ act has trailed through loss, famine journeys, detention, recognition, and restored sight; it follows Joseph’s no-reproach declaration but seeks the father’s intercession separately. The packet supplies that long aftermath; I infer that plural *dhunūb* gathers deeds together with consequences still requiring repair. The ayah reads confession as catching up with the tail of the original act.
reader_a.retrospective_surprises_md: Later 12:100 gathers the family around the realized dream, giving the long trailing consequences of the brothers' sin a repaired social endpoint without pretending those consequences never occurred.

branches.source_phrase_ar: أخطأ إذا لم يصب الصواب؛ الخطأ ما لم يتعمد؛ خطأته تخطئة (ayn)؛ الخطأ نقيض الصواب؛ المخطئ من أراد الصواب فصار إلى غيره؛ خطأته تخطئة وتخطيئا (sihah)؛ أخطأ إذا لم يصب الصواب؛ أخطأت لما صنعه خطأ غير عمد؛ خطىء عنك السوء إذا دعوا له أن يدفع عنه السوء (tahdhib)؛ الخطأ العدول عن الجهة؛ يقع منه خلاف ما يريد؛ أصاب الخطأ وأخطأ الصواب (mufradat)؛ الخطاء مجاوزة حد الصواب؛ أخطأ إذا تعدى الصواب (maqayis)

identity_judgment.rationale: Dal çerçevesi, kaynak ifadesindeki bilerek sakıncalı olana yönelme, günah işleme ve bu eylemden dolayı sorumlu tutulma bileşenlerini doğru biçimde birleştirir. Büyük günah ve günahı işleyen kişi anlamları bu ahlaki çekirdeğin özel görünümleridir.

lexicalization_scope.note: Temel alan kasıtlı ve sorumluluk doğuran kötü eylemdir; eyleyen kişi, büyük günah, çoğul ve ünlem değeri taşıyan türemiş biçimler kendi dil bilgisel sınırlarında tutulur.

concept_map.definition: Kişinin yanlış ve sakıncalı olduğunu bilerek yöneldiği, bu yüzden kınanıp sorumlu tutulduğu günah veya kötü eylemdir. Türemiş kullanımlar eylemi yapan kişiyi, günahların çoğulluğunu ve özellikle ağır günahı belirtebilir.

facets.statement: Kişi yapılmaması gereken bir eyleme bilerek yönelir ve günah işler.
Eylem tamamlanmış bir yanlış sayılır ve kişi bundan dolayı sorumlu tutulur.
Türemiş bir ad, günaha kasıtla yönelen veya yapılmaması gerekeni bilerek yapan kişiyi gösterir.
Bazı kullanımlarda adlandırılan eylem özellikle büyük ve ağır bir günahtır.

source_synthesis.common_summary: Kaynakların ortak çerçevesi günah, suç ve ahlaki bakımdan kötü eylem anlamında birleşir. Bazı açıklama ve kullanımlarda eyleme bilerek yönelme, bundan sorumlu tutulma, eyleyeni gösteren ad ve büyük günah özelleşmesi ayrıca belirtilir.
